question: Can you follow the descending harmony without asking the melody to move faster?
intro: A few repeated melody notes rest above an accompaniment that keeps changing by small steps. Ivan Ilić’s performance of the E-minor Prelude offers a short study in harmonic attention: the quiet middle voices carry much of the motion even when the tune seems almost still.

sections.label: A′ · Renewed phrase
sections.mNote: the opening shape returns and grows more urgent

cues.title: Small movement, changing harmony
cues.text: The melody begins with very little movement, while the repeated accompaniment changes underneath it. Listen inside those chords: small shifts between voices create a sense of descent without requiring a busy tune.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski describes the semitone motif and slow, terse construction: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/197. General opening texture, not a claim that the bass descends on every chord.

cues.title: The Mallorca winter
cues.text: Chopin completed the Op. 28 collection during the winter of 1838–39, spent with George Sand and her children in Mallorca. Some ideas were older; the place of completion does not establish a literal scene behind each Prelude.

cues.title: Follow an inner voice
cues.text: Choose one note within the accompanying chord and listen for where it seems to move next. The harmony changes through voices shifting by small intervals, not through all the notes descending together in parallel.
cues.evidence: Listening invitation to the chromatic accompaniment; no individual note is aligned to this timestamp.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Bach within reach
cues.text: Chopin had Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier with him in Mallorca. His own preludes likewise traverse all major and minor keys, but they do not copy Bach’s chromatic ordering or require a following fugue.
cues.evidence: NIFC prelude overview documents Bach’s collection and the different ordering: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/gatunki/12_preludia

cues.title: A phrase gathers weight
cues.text: The renewed phrase rises towards the main crest before drawing back. Listen for how a modest melodic range can gain urgency through harmonic pressure, fuller sound and closer-spaced activity.
cues.evidence: Report shows a rise around0:50–1:05 followed by a marked fall around1:10. This anchors the broad crest, not a precise written dynamic or harmonic event.

cues.title: A complete miniature
cues.text: The fourth Prelude is an independent piece within a set of twenty-four. Chopin turns a form associated with introductory playing into music that can make a complete statement in only a few phrases.
cues.evidence: The autonomous character of the Op.28 preludes, in contrast to earlier preluding practice: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/gatunki/12_preludia

cues.title: The final space matters
cues.text: The closing chords follow a withdrawal and a pause. Listen to the silence and decay as part of the phrase’s ending; do not mistake the absence of new attacks for an invitation to hurry the final resolution.
cues.evidence: Report novelty near1:30 and low onset density in the closing windows support a passage-level close. No exact fermata length or pedal technique is claimed.

transitions.title: The opening shape returns under pressure
transitions.how: The first phrase’s descent leads to a renewal of the opening melodic shape. The accompaniment continues to change by small voice-leading steps, but the new phrase grows towards a stronger crest. Familiar material becomes more urgent through harmonic and dynamic intensification rather than through an unrelated contrasting tune.
transitions.evidence: Approximate phrase renewal near0:48; report activity increases around0:50 and builds to the1:00–1:05 crest. The semitone-based design is described by https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/197

transitions.title: The descending phrase leaves space for closure
transitions.how: The renewed phrase loses force and the chordal motion is interrupted by a pause. The final chords then complete the cadence rather than launching another phrase. The contrast between the earlier repeating pulse and the sparse ending makes the resolution feel deliberately delayed.
transitions.evidence: Approximate closing boundary at1:30, with reduced onset density and quiet late windows; a passage marker, not a measured fermata onset.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
